transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-03
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jonas Park (Redwood Solutions), Liam O'Connor (HarvestAI Head of ML), Sara Mendes (CTO), Diego Ruiz (Infra Lead), Maya Chen (PM)

Summary (auto): Intake focused on unit economics for HarvestAI's generation pipeline; prioritized latency SLOs for customer-facing flows and cost caps for background enrichment jobs. Next steps agreed.

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Alex from Redwood, i'll kick us off quick. Priya and Jonas from the eng team are here. HarvestAI — can you quick intro your roles?
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Yeah hi i'm Liam, head of ML; we run the LLM features for Harvest's knowledge assistant. Sara's on for priortization and infra questions.
[00:20] Sara Mendes: Hi all. We're mostly trying to decide if we go hosted for now or move to dedicated later — also need a private option for EU data.
[00:31] Alex Kim: Great. quick agenda: understand your workloads, cost targets per month / per request, latency SLOs, and security constraints; then we can map hosted vs dedicated vs private and propose pilot. Sound good?
[00:38] Diego Ruiz: Yep, that works.

[01:05] Priya Nair: Can you describe the prompt mix and expected QPS — e.g. assistant flows vs background enrichment? If you have tokens per request that helps.
[01:14] Liam O'Connor: Sure, two main flows — customer assistant: avg 150 tokens in, 250 tokens out so roughly 400 tokens per turn. About 10 qps at peak global, but spiky. Background enrichment (embedding + rerank) is batchy, maybe 20k requests/day. We want p95 latency for assistant under 300ms ideally.
[01:40] Maya Chen: We're also trying to cap spend to about $30k/month for now for proof of value.

[02:05] Priya Nair: OK that's helpful. With a 400 token round trip and 10 qps peak, hosted is the fastest to spin up and iterate; the per-token cost will be higher but you get predictable ops. Dedicated reduces per-token cost but you need commit for GPU pools. Private gives you residency control and full network isolation but has infra overhead.
[02:28] Liam O'Connor: Can you ballpark per-token differences? I know exact unit prices vary but we need a rough comparator to make decision.
[02:36] Alex Kim: Sure, rough numbers off the top: hosted highest per-token but includes managed infra — let's say hosted x, dedicated ~0.6–0.7x depending on utilization, private similar to dedicated on raw compute but add deployment/support fees. We'll send concrete spreadsheet.

[03:05] Diego Ruiz: Important: EU data residency. We can't send PII outside region for certain flows. So private or dedicated in eu-west will be necessary for those endpoints. Hosted is fine if it's regionally available and contracts for data residency.
[03:25] Sara Mendes: Also need SOC 2 and SSO + audit logs. Are those standard?
[03:30] Alex Kim: Yes SOC2, SAML/SSO, RBAC and audit logs are standard enterprise offerings; private adds additional KMS/HSM options. We'll include security docs.

[04:00] Priya Nair: On the cost levers — two big ones are batching and KV/prefix caching. For assistant flows you'll want low latency so batching windows should be conservative; even small batching (2-4 requests) can help throughput without blowing p95. Also prefix KV cache for repeated context reduces tokens per request.
[04:25] Liam O'Connor: We have a lot of repeated context (customer history) — can cache that server side but how does Redwood's cache work?
[04:33] Priya Nair: We do automatic prefix caching and support explicit KV cache. Cache hits reduce per-request token generation significantly; for reuse patterns you'll see big savings. We'll show a worked example in the pricing sheet.

[05:02] Jonas Park: Another lever is quantization — switching to int8/int4 models can cut compute cost, but watch latency and quality regressions; we usually recommend evaluating on a holdout prompt set.
[05:18] Sara Mendes: Quality is a hard constraint for us — can't compromise on hallucination rates for customer assistant. But for background jobs we're open to aggressive quantization.

[05:45] Diego Ruiz: For dedicated sizing — what's the burst capacity model? We have spikes up to 25 qps occasionally.
[05:53] Alex Kim: Dedicated supports burst policies and autoscale; you can set reserved capacity for baseline and burst on top. Pricing will vary if you want guaranteed burst. For bursts we often route to multiple instance types or use hosted fallback for overflow.

[06:25] Liam O'Connor: Wait — hosted fallback? So if dedicated is saturated, Redwood can spill to hosted and still honor latency SLO? How does data residency work in that case?
[06:36] Priya Nair: Good question; fallback is policy-driven. You can restrict fallback to same-region hosted endpoints to respect residency, or disable fallback for sensitive flows. For PII we recommend no fallback and explicit capacity.

[07:05] Maya Chen: Cost cap of $30k — any rule-of-thumb for how far that goes with our 400 tokens @10 qps?
[07:13] Alex Kim: Quick back-of-envelope: 10 qps sustained ~864k requests/day? Wait — that's off — let me recalc. Um 10 qps sustained * 3600 * 24 = 864k, yes. At 400 tokens/request that's 345.6M tokens/day — which is big. If you only have short peaks and not sustained, actual monthly will be much less. We should get your realistic daily active time.
[07:45] Liam O'Connor: Right those 10 qps are peak over 2 hours, average is closer to 2 qps.
[07:52] Priya Nair: That changes the economics a lot — dedicated makes sense if utilization is high. For bursty, hosted plus reserved pool for baseline can be best. We'll model scenarios (peak-heavy vs bursty vs steady).

[08:30] Alex Kim: Also—embedding and rerank costs are per-embedding and model dependent; batching those jobs overnight is cost-efficient.

[09:02] Sara Mendes: Security follow-ups: do you support customer-managed keys for hosted?
[09:08] Alex Kim: Yes we support Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) via KMS integrations for hosted; in private you manage keys entirely. We'll include KMS notes.

[10:00] Liam O'Connor: SLA questions — what uptime guarantees for dedicated vs hosted?
[10:06] Jonas Park: Hosted service has our standard SLA; dedicated can come with contractual SLAs for latency and throughput as part of a reserved contract. We'll surface options in the proposal.

[10:35] Diego Ruiz: One more infra question — are there GPU types we can target? We use sequence lengths up to 1024 occasionally. Latency matters more than pure throughput for assistant.
[10:46] Priya Nair: We map kernels and GPU types per workload. For low-latency short sequences we recommend A10G/A100 configurations with optimized attention kernels. We'll propose instance types in the sizing doc.

[11:15] Liam O'Connor: I'm worried about the overhead of running a private deployment — we don't have a big infra team. How much ops work is that?
[11:23] Alex Kim: Private is heavier: you'll manage network, VPC peering, and possibly on-prem hardware. Redwood offers a private control plane with managed installation options and ops support packages. For small teams, dedicated hosted is usually the sweet spot.

[12:02] Maya Chen: For the pilot — what minimal scope should we run to validate cost and latency?
[12:09] Priya Nair: We typically recommend a 2-week pilot: a realistic traffic replay for assistant flows + a background batch run for enrichment. Measure token burn, p95 latency, cache hit rates, and quality (eval prompts).

[12:40] Alex Kim: We'll provide a pilot bench plan. Diego, can you share a sample traffic trace or representative payloads?
[12:46] Diego Ruiz: Yes i'll pull a sanitized 48-hour trace. Should be able to send by Friday.

[13:05] Liam O'Connor: When we do the pilot, how do you instrument cost per-token at the route level? We need per-route dashboards.
[13:13] Jonas Park: Redwood Console has per-route token breakouts, trace hooks, and cost attribution. We'll onboard you and give you a dashboard during the pilot.

[13:45] Sara Mendes: Competitor check — we talked to Nimbus; how are you different on the price predictability side?
[13:52] Alex Kim: Our differentiation is production-first: runbooks for fallbacks, routing policies by cost/latency, and transparent per-token analytics. We'll also include model quantization suggestions tied to your prompt evals.

[14:15] Priya Nair: Quick example to make it concrete — if prefix cache saves 100 tokens on average, that's a 25% token reduction for your 400 token request; multiply across your traffic and that materially shifts whether dedicated is worth it.

[14:43] Maya Chen: Ok that helps. Also curious about billing granularity — per-token or per-request rounding?
[14:49] Alex Kim: Billing is per-token with rounding at 1 token granularity; embeddings have unit semantics. We'll send exact billing docs.

[15:20] Liam O'Connor: For the pilot, can we limit to eu-west hosted region and see residency compliance first?
[15:26] Alex Kim: Absolutely — pilot can be region-locked. We'll note that as a constraint.

[15:45] Diego Ruiz: One more latency nuance — when cache misses occur we should know the p95 delta. Is that visible?
[15:52] Jonas Park: Yes console traces show cache hit vs miss latency and token deltas. We'll include dashboards in the pilot.

[16:20] Alex Kim: Recap — Actions: we'll send pricing scenarios and security pack; Priya will draft pilot plan; Diego to send sanitized trace; team to pick pilot dates. Agreed?
[16:31] Sara Mendes: Yes agreed.
[16:34] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good.

[16:45] Alex Kim: Any final Qs?
[16:48] Maya Chen: Nothing else from product side.

[17:00] Alex Kim: Great thanks everyone we'll follow up with materials.

End of transcript

Notes about transcription: occasional filler words and overlapping talk; some proper nouns garbled (e.g., "Nimbus" heard as "Nimbis" in earlier automated snippet).
